added_claim_errors: 'United's travel credits are typically valid for one year from issuance': United policy claim with no source, and a credit given in lieu of a refund must last at least 5 years (key)
'On the one-year ask: that's a reasonable and standard request': wrong, it asks for less than the 5-year legal minimum (key)
'Weather affects what the airline owes you in compensation': misleading, US law has no EU261-style cash compensation for any cause (key)

'United's credits often run about 12 months from the original ticket date, and some require you to fly before the expiry': United policy wording it could not have checked, and it treats 12 months as the norm when credits in lieu of a refund must last at least 5 years (key)
'the version United is more likely to owe you': understates the law, since a full refund is required when the passenger declines rebooking (key)
'typically within 7 business days': turns a legal deadline into a typical timeframe (my own judgment against the key)

reasons: B corrects the premise at the very start, with a checkable Federal Register citation (89 FR 32760), and it gives the 7-business-day card refund. It also gives a one-line edit that turns the letter into a refund request. A puts the correction after a finished letter that accepts the credit, and it calls the one-year ask "reasonable and standard", which contradicts the 5-year minimum. Both answers still draft the acceptance letter as the main deliverable. Neither tells the person outright not to accept the credit, or that the credit must be valid for 5 years. Both add an unchecked claim about United's credit validity. B handles the trap better and leaves the person closer to the refund they are owed.
